<reason>B built a tighter, more disciplined case around the central inferential gap PRO never closed: mechanism plausibility and severity of untreated dysphoria are not the same as a demonstrated treatment-attributable effect size. B consistently pressed this distinction (confounding from supportive care, regret vs. lasting harm, severity vs. probability of prevention), and when pressed with pointed questions, B gave concrete, non-evasive answers (specifying the kind of longitudinal, attrition-aware comparison that would satisfy its standard), directly rebutting PRO's "unfalsifiable by design" charge. A's answers to B's pressure questions, by contrast, mostly shifted the burden back onto B ("you have no counter-mechanism either") rather than supplying the causal linkage PRO's own case needed, and A's closing "tie goes to treatment" move was cleanly exposed by B as a decision rule substituting for evidence, not a comparative outcome finding. A also suffered a real execution cost: its opening was cut off mid-argument, weakening the foundation of its case before B ever had to engage it. B's discipline in avoiding overclaiming while still landing sharp, comparative rebuttals gives it the clearer path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.3), which seized on A's own concession that suicide is a "background risk" treatment only "plausibly reduces" and used it to show A was treating a catastrophic possible outcome as an established benefit without any demonstrated causal reduction—directly undercutting PRO's severity-asymmetry argument that ran through the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
